board_events.text: Solid: caged and vibrating. Liquid: touching but sliding. Gas: far apart and free.
Same particles; only the spacing and the forces change.
Feynman: everything is made of atoms, tiny particles in perpetual motion.

segments.text: <curious>Let us begin</curious> with the single founding idea that this whole chapter unpacks: all matter is made of enormous numbers of tiny particles, atoms and molecules, in perpetual motion.

This is the atomic hypothesis. The thinker Kanada and the Greek Democritus guessed at indivisible particles long ago, but it was Dalton, in the early eighteen hundreds, who turned the idea into testable chemistry.

Dalton's theory makes three claims. Matter is built from atoms. All atoms of a given element are identical in mass and properties. And atoms combine only in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds, which is why a compound always holds the same elements in the same fixed mass ratio.
Now zoom into a steel rod, a cup of water, and the air above it. You find the very same building blocks, molecules, but arranged in completely different ways.

In the solid they are packed shoulder to shoulder, locked in a rigid lattice, only jiggling in place. In the liquid they still touch but slide past one another, which is why a liquid flows. In the gas they are flung far apart, about ten times farther, racing almost independently.
Hold onto that. Same particles, three states, and the only thing that truly changes is how close the molecules sit and how strongly they feel one another.

Feynman once said that if all of science were compressed to one sentence, the most valuable would be that everything is made of atoms, tiny particles in perpetual motion. Almost this whole chapter is just that sentence, unpacked.
चलिए उस एक founding idea से शुरू करते हैं जिस पर पूरा chapter टिका है: हर matter अनगिनत tiny particles से बना है, यानी atoms और molecules, जो हमेशा perpetual motion में रहते हैं।
इसे atomic hypothesis कहते हैं। Kanada और Greek Democritus ने बहुत पहले indivisible particles का अंदाज़ा लगाया था, पर Dalton ने early eighteen hundreds में इसे testable chemistry में बदल दिया।

Dalton की theory तीन बातें कहती है। Matter atoms से बना है। किसी एक element के सारे atoms mass और properties में एक जैसे होते हैं। और atoms सिर्फ़ simple whole-number ratios में मिलकर compounds बनाते हैं, इसीलिए एक compound में हमेशा वही elements उसी fixed mass ratio में होते हैं।
अब एक steel rod, एक cup पानी, और ऊपर की हवा में zoom करके देखिए। आपको वही same building blocks मिलेंगे, molecules, बस उनका arrangement बिलकुल अलग होगा।

Solid में वे shoulder to shoulder packed होते हैं, एक rigid lattice में बंधे, बस अपनी जगह जिगल करते हैं। Liquid में touching तो रहते हैं पर एक-दूसरे के पास से slide करते हैं, इसलिए liquid बहता है। Gas में वे बहुत दूर, करीब दस गुना दूर, लगभग independently दौड़ते हैं।
इसे पकड़ के रखिए। Same particles, तीन states, और असल में सिर्फ़ यही बदलता है कि molecules कितने पास बैठे हैं और एक-दूसरे को कितनी strongly feel करते हैं।

<excited>Feynman ने कहा था</excited> कि अगर पूरी science को एक sentence में समेटना हो, तो सबसे valuable यही होगा कि everything atoms से बना है, tiny particles जो perpetual motion में हैं। लगभग पूरा chapter बस इसी sentence का unpacking है।

board_events.text: What decides the spacing? The intermolecular force
Weak attraction when moderately apart; strong repulsion when pushed too close.
In between lies a special separation $r_0$ where attraction and repulsion cancel: net force is zero.

board_events.text: At $r_0$ the PE is a minimum (most stable); small pushes give a restoring force.
In a gas, molecules are far beyond force range until the instant they collide.
Heat a solid: vibrations grow, the lattice melts to liquid, then frees to gas.

segments.text: <curious>What decides</curious> how close molecules sit is the intermolecular force between them. It has two competing sides, and the balance between them sets everything.

Two molecules attract each other weakly when they are a moderate distance apart, and this weak pull is what holds liquids and solids together. But push them too close and they repel fiercely, because you cannot force two molecules into the same space.

Somewhere in between lies a special separation, written r nought, where attraction and repulsion cancel exactly and the net force is zero. This is the comfortable equilibrium spacing that molecules in a solid settle into.

Here is the picture. The red curve is the force and the blue dashed curve is the potential energy, both plotted against separation. On the steep inner wall the force is repulsive; on the gentle outer side it is attractive.
The force is minus the slope of the potential energy: F equals minus d U by d r. So where the potential energy curve bottoms out, its slope is zero, and the force passes through zero right there.

At r nought the potential energy is a minimum, the most stable point, and any small displacement produces a restoring force. That is exactly why atoms in a solid vibrate about fixed sites instead of drifting away or collapsing inward.

And here is why a gas is the natural home of kinetic theory. Its molecules sit so far apart that, for almost their whole lives, they are beyond the reach of these forces and feel essentially nothing until the instant they collide.

One more thread ties the states together. Add heat to a solid and the vibrations about r nought grow until the lattice breaks down into a liquid, and more heat frees the molecules entirely into a gas.
molecules कितने पास बैठेंगे यह intermolecular force तय करती है। इसके दो competing sides हैं, और उनका balance ही सब कुछ set करता है।

दो molecules moderate distance पर हल्की सी attract करते हैं, और यही weak pull liquids और solids को साथ बांधे रखती है। पर उन्हें बहुत पास धकेलिए तो वे ज़ोर से repel करते हैं, क्योंकि दो molecules को एक ही जगह में force नहीं किया जा सकता।

इन दोनों के बीच एक special separation होती है, जिसे r nought लिखते हैं, जहाँ attraction और repulsion बिलकुल cancel हो जाते हैं और net force zero होती है। यही वह comfortable equilibrium spacing है जिसमें solid के molecules बैठ जाते हैं।
यह रहा picture. लाल curve force है और नीली dashed curve potential energy, दोनों separation के against plot हैं। steep inner wall पर force repulsive है; gentle outer side पर attractive।
Force potential energy के slope का minus है: F बराबर minus d U by d r। तो जहाँ potential energy curve सबसे नीचे झुकती है, वहाँ उसका slope zero होता है, और force ठीक वहीं zero से गुज़रती है।

r nought पर potential energy minimum है, सबसे stable point, और कोई भी छोटा displacement एक restoring force पैदा करता है। इसीलिए solid के atoms fixed sites के आस-पास vibrate करते हैं, न कि दूर चले जाते हैं या अंदर collapse होते हैं।

और इसीलिए gas kinetic theory का natural घर है। इसके molecules इतने दूर बैठे होते हैं कि लगभग पूरी ज़िंदगी वे इन forces की पहुँच से बाहर रहते हैं और collide करने के पल तक essentially कुछ feel नहीं करते।

एक और thread इन states को जोड़ता है। solid को heat दीजिए तो r nought के आस-पास की vibrations बढ़ती जाती हैं जब तक lattice टूटकर liquid न बन जाए, और और heat molecules को पूरी तरह free करके gas बना देती है।

board_events.text: Smaller particle, higher temperature: a more violent dance.
Diffusion: ink in water, scent across a room, driven by random thermal motion.
Oil-film: a drop spreads one molecule thick; volume over area gives molecular size ~10^-9 to 10^-10 m.
Definite proportions: simple whole-number reacting ratios point to discrete atoms.

segments.text: We cannot see molecules, so how do we know they are really moving? Three pieces of everyday evidence make the case, and the most direct is Brownian motion.

In eighteen twenty seven the botanist Robert Brown noticed that tiny pollen grains suspended in still water jiggled about ceaselessly along random, erratic paths, even though the water was perfectly calm.
Look closely at what is happening. The grain is far too big to move on its own; what jostles it is the relentless bombardment of invisible water molecules striking it unevenly from every side.

The smaller the particle and the higher the temperature, the more violent the dance. So Brownian motion is a visible fingerprint of the unseen molecular motion that kinetic theory assumes, a bridge from the microscopic world to something you can watch under a microscope.
The same idea explains diffusion. A drop of ink spreading through still water, or a whiff of perfume crossing a room, is molecules wandering and mixing purely because of their random thermal motion.

A third clue lets us size a molecule. In the oil-film experiment a tiny drop of oil spreads on water until it is just one molecule thick, and from the known volume and the measured area we get the molecular size, around a nanometre down to an angstrom.

And there is a chemical clue too. Substances react in simple whole-number ratios, which only makes sense if matter comes in discrete atomic units. Four different windows, one conclusion: matter is molecular, and its molecules move.
<curious>हम molecules देख नहीं सकते</curious>, तो कैसे पता कि वे सच में move करते हैं? तीन everyday evidence इसे साबित करते हैं, और सबसे direct है Brownian motion।
eighteen twenty seven में botanist Robert Brown ने देखा कि still पानी में suspended tiny pollen grains लगातार random, erratic paths पर jiggle करते रहते हैं, जबकि पानी बिलकुल calm था।
ध्यान से देखिए क्या हो रहा है। grain अपने आप हिलने के लिए बहुत बड़ा है; उसे जो jostle करता है वह है invisible water molecules की relentless bombardment, जो हर side से unevenly टकराते हैं।

particle जितना छोटा और temperature जितना ज़्यादा, dance उतना violent। तो Brownian motion उस unseen molecular motion का visible fingerprint है जिसे kinetic theory मानती है, microscopic दुनिया से उस चीज़ तक का bridge जिसे आप microscope के नीचे देख सकते हैं।
यही idea diffusion को समझाता है। still पानी में फैलती ink की एक बूँद, या कमरे में फैलती perfume की खुशबू, यह molecules का wandering और mixing है, सिर्फ़ उनकी random thermal motion की वजह से।

एक तीसरा clue molecule की size बताता है। oil-film experiment में oil की एक tiny drop पानी पर फैलकर बस एक molecule मोटी हो जाती है, और known volume तथा measured area से हमें molecular size मिलती है, करीब एक nanometre से लेकर एक angstrom तक।

और एक chemical clue भी है। पदार्थ simple whole-number ratios में react करते हैं, जो तभी sense बनाता है जब matter discrete atomic units में आए। चार अलग windows, एक ही conclusion: matter molecular है और उसके molecules move करते हैं।

segments.text: Kinetic theory keeps insisting a gas is mostly empty. Let us make that quantitative with two quick estimation recipes, the same moves that turn up again and again in problems.

First, the number density, how many molecules sit in each unit of volume. From the ideal gas law it is the pressure divided by Boltzmann's constant times temperature, or equivalently one mole in twenty two point four litres at S T P.

The average volume owned by one molecule is one over the number density, and the mean separation between molecules is roughly the cube root of that volume. For a gas at S T P this comes out about ten times the molecular diameter.

This diagram is worth memorising. Carry three numbers in your head: the molecular size, about ten to the minus ten metres; the gas spacing, roughly ten times that; and the mean free path, roughly a thousand times the molecular size.

Notice these are different quantities. The spacing is the gap to your nearest neighbour; the mean free path is the far larger distance you fly before hitting anyone. Confusing the two is one of the most common slips in this topic.

The second recipe checks the emptiness directly. Model each molecule as a sphere, multiply its volume by Avogadro's number to get the molecular volume in a mole, and divide by the actual molar volume. The ratio comes out around ten to the minus three or ten to the minus four, the tiny fraction the molecules actually fill.
So keep the mantra: <whisper>size, spacing, free path</whisper>, each about ten times the one before. Most conceptual questions in this section fall apart the moment you compare these three scales.
kinetic theory बार-बार कहती है कि gas ज़्यादातर empty है। चलिए इसे दो quick estimation recipes से quantitative बनाते हैं, वही moves जो problems में बार-बार आते हैं।

पहला, number density, यानी हर unit volume में कितने molecules बैठे हैं। ideal gas law से यह pressure बटा Boltzmann constant into temperature है, या फिर S T P पर एक mole in twenty two point four litres।

एक molecule के हिस्से का average volume number density का inverse है, और molecules के बीच mean separation लगभग उस volume का cube root है। S T P पर gas के लिए यह molecular diameter का करीब दस गुना निकलता है।
यह diagram याद करने लायक है। दिमाग़ में तीन numbers रखिए: molecular size, करीब ten to the minus ten metres; gas spacing, उसका करीब दस गुना; और mean free path, molecular size का करीब हज़ार गुना।

ध्यान दीजिए ये अलग quantities हैं। spacing आपके nearest neighbour तक का gap है; mean free path वह कहीं बड़ी दूरी है जो आप किसी से टकराने से पहले fly करते हैं। इन दोनों को confuse करना इस topic की सबसे common गलतियों में से है।

दूसरी recipe emptiness को सीधे check करती है। हर molecule को एक sphere मानिए, उसके volume को Avogadro number से multiply करके एक mole का molecular volume निकालिए, और actual molar volume से divide कीजिए। ratio करीब ten to the minus three या ten to the minus four निकलता है, container का वह tiny fraction जो molecules असल में भरते हैं।
तो mantra याद रखिए: size, spacing, free path, हर एक पिछले से करीब दस गुना। इस section के ज़्यादातर conceptual questions इन तीन scales को compare करते ही solve हो जाते हैं।

segments.text: Here is a board-level estimate. In one mole of oxygen gas at S T P, what fraction of the total volume is actually occupied by the molecules themselves? Take the diameter of an oxygen molecule to be three angstrom.
Picture it first. The container is almost entirely empty, with the molecules as sparse specks, and the bar on the right previews just how thin the filled sliver will be.

Set out the data. The radius is half the diameter, one point five times ten to the minus ten metres. The molar volume at S T P is twenty two point four times ten to the minus three cubic metres. And Avogadro's number is six point zero two two times ten to the twenty third.
The molecular volume in one mole is Avogadro's number times the volume of one sphere, four thirds pi r cubed.

Plugging in, one sphere is about one point four one times ten to the minus twenty nine cubic metres, and multiplying by Avogadro's number gives roughly eight point five times ten to the minus six cubic metres of actual molecular matter.
Divide by the molar volume and the fraction is about three point eight times ten to the minus four.

So only about four in ten thousand, roughly four hundredths of a percent, of the gas's volume is actually molecules. That tiny number is the quantitative reason we may treat gas molecules as point masses.

एक mole में molecular volume Avogadro number into एक sphere का volume है, four thirds pi r cubed।

plug करने पर, एक sphere करीब one point four one times ten to the minus twenty nine cubic metres है, और Avogadro number से multiply करने पर actual molecular matter करीब eight point five times ten to the minus six cubic metres निकलता है।
molar volume से divide कीजिए और fraction करीब three point eight times ten to the minus four आता है।

तो gas के volume का सिर्फ़ करीब four in ten thousand, यानी करीब four hundredths of a percent, असल में molecules है। यही tiny number वह quantitative वजह है जिससे हम gas molecules को point masses मान सकते हैं।

segments.text: A classic N E E T speed trap. Under the same temperature and pressure, three litres of hydrogen react completely with oxygen to form water vapour. The balanced reaction is two hydrogen plus one oxygen gives two water. Find the oxygen consumed and the water vapour produced.
The whole problem is in this picture. Because equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, the volumes react in the very same ratio as the molecules, two to one to two.
So skip the moles entirely. The oxygen volume is half the hydrogen volume, because the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is two to one.
Half of three litres is one point five litres of oxygen consumed.
And the water vapour matches the hydrogen, two to two, so three litres of water vapour are produced.
Oxygen one point five litres, water vapour three litres. Two lines, no calculator needed.

Now the trap. Students often expect total volume to be conserved and add three plus one point five to guess four point five litres of product. <chuckle>That is wrong.</chuckle> Volume is not conserved in gaseous reactions; the balanced equation and molecule count rule, not the sum of volumes.

एक classic N E E T speed trap. same temperature और pressure पर, three litres hydrogen पूरी तरह oxygen के साथ react करके water vapour बनाती है। balanced reaction है two hydrogen plus one oxygen gives two water। oxygen consumed और water vapour produced निकालिए।
पूरा problem इसी picture में है। चूँकि equal volumes में equal number of molecules होते हैं, volumes उसी ratio में react करते हैं जिसमें molecules, two to one to two।
तो moles को छोड़ ही दीजिए। oxygen का volume hydrogen के आधा है, क्योंकि hydrogen to oxygen ratio two to one है।
three litres का आधा one point five litres oxygen consumed है।
और water vapour hydrogen से match करता है, two to two, तो three litres water vapour produce होती है।
Oxygen one point five litres, water vapour three litres। दो lines, कोई calculator नहीं।

अब trap। students अक्सर सोचते हैं total volume conserve होगा और three plus one point five जोड़कर four point five litres product का अंदाज़ा लगाते हैं। यह ग़लत है। gaseous reactions में volume conserve नहीं होता, balanced equation और molecule count चलते हैं, volumes का sum नहीं।

segments.text: <curious>A J E E Main favourite.</curious> Estimate the mean separation between molecules of an ideal gas at S T P, and compare it with a molecular diameter of three angstrom.
The recipe is number density first, then the cube-root spacing. At S T P one mole, that is Avogadro's number of molecules, occupies twenty two point four times ten to the minus three cubic metres.
Divide the molar volume by Avogadro's number and each molecule owns about three point seven two times ten to the minus twenty six cubic metres.
The mean separation is the cube root of that volume, about three point three four times ten to the minus nine metres, which is thirty three point four angstrom.
Picture that against the molecule itself. The gap between neighbours is far wider than a molecule is big.
Divide the separation by the diameter and you get about eleven. Molecules sit, on average, eleven diameters apart.
That is the concrete meaning of the phrase gas spacing is about ten times the spacing in a solid, and it is exactly why intermolecular forces are negligible in a gas.
एक J E E Main favourite. S T P पर एक ideal gas के molecules के बीच mean separation estimate कीजिए, और उसे three angstrom के molecular diameter से compare कीजिए।

mean separation उस volume का cube root है, करीब three point three four times ten to the minus nine metres, यानी thirty three point four angstrom।
इसे molecule के मुक़ाबले picture कीजिए। neighbours के बीच का gap molecule की size से कहीं ज़्यादा चौड़ा है।

segments.text: <curious>Now the advanced version.</curious> Liquid nitrogen has a density of about eight hundred ten kilograms per cubic metre and a molar mass of twenty eight grams per mole. Find the number density, the mean spacing, and compare it with nitrogen gas at S T P, where the spacing was about thirty three angstrom.
The move is the same recipe as before, just run backwards. From a measured density, recover how tightly the molecules are packed, then take the cube root for their spacing.
Number density is density times Avogadro's number over molar mass. That gives about one point seven four times ten to the twenty eight molecules per cubic metre, a thousandfold denser than the gas.
The spacing is the inverse cube root of that, about three point nine times ten to the minus ten metres, roughly three point nine angstrom.

Set the two side by side. In the liquid the molecules are about three point nine angstrom apart, essentially touching, since that is close to a molecular diameter. In the gas they were about thirty three angstrom apart.
So liquefaction pulls the molecules roughly eight to nine times closer, from far apart and free to touching and interacting.

And that is precisely why the ideal gas model fails for a liquid. The intermolecular forces that were negligible in the gas now dominate completely, because the molecules are packed right up against one another.

अब advanced version. liquid nitrogen की density करीब eight hundred ten kilograms per cubic metre है और molar mass twenty eight grams per mole। number density, mean spacing निकालिए, और S T P पर nitrogen gas से compare कीजिए, जहाँ spacing करीब thirty three angstrom था।
यह वही recipe है, बस उल्टा चलाया गया। एक measured density से पता लगाइए कि molecules कितने tightly packed हैं, फिर उनकी spacing के लिए cube root लीजिए।
number density density into Avogadro number बटा molar mass है। यह करीब one point seven four times ten to the twenty eight molecules per cubic metre देता है, gas से हज़ार गुना denser।
spacing उसका inverse cube root है, करीब three point nine times ten to the minus ten metres, यानी करीब three point nine angstrom।
दोनों को साथ रखिए। liquid में molecules करीब three point nine angstrom दूर हैं, essentially touching, क्योंकि यह एक molecular diameter के करीब है। gas में वे करीब thirty three angstrom दूर थे।
तो liquefaction molecules को करीब आठ से नौ गुना पास खींच लाता है, far apart and free से touching and interacting तक।
और ठीक इसीलिए ideal gas model liquid के लिए fail होता है। जो intermolecular forces gas में negligible थीं, वे अब पूरी तरह dominate करती हैं, क्योंकि molecules एक-दूसरे से बिलकुल सटे होते हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: molecular nature

board_events.text: Pitfalls to avoid, and one pro-tip
Do not confuse molecular spacing (~10x diameter) with mean free path (~1000x diameter).
Combining volumes follow the balanced equation, not conservation of total volume.
Molecules do not only attract: without short-range repulsion, matter would collapse.
A gas is ~99.96% empty space at STP; picturing it as densely packed misleads.
Brownian motion is indirect: you see the grain dance, not the molecules.
Pro-tip: carry size ~1e-10 m, spacing ~10x, mean free path ~1000x; most questions fall to a scale comparison.

segments.text: Before we move on, here are the traps this section is built to catch, and one pro-tip that answers most of its questions.

First and biggest: do not confuse molecular spacing with the mean free path. The spacing to your nearest neighbour is about ten diameters; the mean free path, the distance flown between collisions, is about a thousand diameters. Different quantities entirely.
Second, do not expect volume to be conserved in a gaseous reaction. Two volumes plus one volume need not give three; the balanced equation and Avogadro's law set the ratios.

Third, do not think molecules only attract. Without the short-range repulsion, matter would simply collapse. The force is repulsive below the equilibrium separation and attractive above it, and both halves are essential.

Fourth, do not picture a gas as full of molecules. It is about ninety nine point nine six percent empty space at S T P, and imagining it densely packed leads to wrong intuitions about how compressible it is.

Fifth, do not misattribute Brownian motion. The jiggling particle you observe is a much larger suspended grain being kicked around by molecules; you see the effect, the grain's dance, never the molecules themselves.

And the pro-tip that ties it together: <whisper>carry those three orders of magnitude in your head</whisper>, molecular size, spacing ten times larger, mean free path a thousand times larger. Most conceptual questions here are answered just by lining up these scales.
<curious>आगे बढ़ने से पहले</curious>, यहाँ वे traps हैं जिन्हें यह section पकड़ने के लिए बना है, और एक pro-tip जो इसके ज़्यादातर questions solve कर देती है।

पहला और सबसे बड़ा: molecular spacing को mean free path से confuse मत कीजिए। nearest neighbour तक की spacing करीब दस diameters है; mean free path, यानी collisions के बीच उड़ी दूरी, करीब हज़ार diameters है। बिलकुल अलग quantities।
दूसरा, gaseous reaction में volume conserve होने की उम्मीद मत कीजिए। two volumes plus one volume ज़रूरी नहीं कि three दें; balanced equation और Avogadro law ratios तय करते हैं।

तीसरा, यह मत सोचिए कि molecules सिर्फ़ attract करते हैं। short-range repulsion के बिना matter बस collapse हो जाता। force equilibrium separation के नीचे repulsive और ऊपर attractive है, और दोनों halves ज़रूरी हैं।
चौथा, gas को molecules से भरा हुआ मत सोचिए। S T P पर यह करीब ninety nine point nine six percent empty space है, और इसे densely packed सोचना compressibility के बारे में गलत intuitions देता है।

पाँचवाँ, Brownian motion को गलत attribute मत कीजिए। जो jiggling particle आप देखते हैं वह एक कहीं बड़ा suspended grain है जिसे molecules इधर-उधर kick करते हैं; आप effect देखते हैं, grain का dance, molecules खुद कभी नहीं।

और वह pro-tip जो सब जोड़ती है: उन तीन orders of magnitude को दिमाग़ में रखिए, molecular size, दस गुना बड़ी spacing, हज़ार गुना बड़ा mean free path। यहाँ के ज़्यादातर conceptual questions बस इन scales को line up करने से हल हो जाते हैं।

board_events.text: Assumptions: point masses, no forces except collisions, all collisions perfectly elastic.
Also: straight-line free flight, identical molecules, gravity ignored, uniform density.
No interaction PE, so an ideal gas's internal energy is purely kinetic energy of motion.

segments.text: <curious>Sub-topic one asks a simpler question:</curious> how does a gas as a whole behave? A real gas is messy, so we invent a clean idealisation, the ideal gas, by stripping the messiness away.

Picture a Mumbai local at nine in the morning, packed, everyone shoving the doors, the push on the walls enormous. Now the same compartment at two in the afternoon, nearly empty, a few people drifting. A gas is exactly this crowd, except the passengers are molecules and the shove they give the walls is what we call pressure.

An ideal gas is a crowd of point-like particles that take up no real volume, exert no force on one another except during instantaneous collisions, and otherwise fly in straight lines. Nothing sticks them together, so an ideal gas has no potential energy of interaction at all.
Here is the mental model: a hall full of perfectly smooth marbles that never attract and never deform. They only knock about and bounce elastically off the walls.

It is worth naming the assumptions, because every later result rests on them. The molecules are point masses whose own volume is negligible against the container. There are no intermolecular forces except during collisions. And all collisions are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is ever lost.

A few more. Between collisions the molecules move freely in straight lines, spending negligible time actually colliding; the gas is a pure substance with identical molecules; and gravity is ignored, so the density is uniform throughout. Strip any one away and you are back to a real gas.

The payoff of this whole picture is one clean statement: because there is no interaction energy, all of an ideal gas's internal energy is the kinetic energy of its molecules' motion. That single fact drives the next two subtopics.
Sub-topic one एक simpler सवाल पूछता है: एक gas as a whole कैसे behave करता है? real gas messy है, तो हम एक clean idealisation बनाते हैं, ideal gas, messiness को हटाकर।

<excited>नौ बजे सुबह की Mumbai local सोचिए</excited>, packed, सब doors पर धक्का, walls पर push ज़बरदस्त। अब वही compartment दोपहर दो बजे, लगभग खाली, कुछ लोग drift करते। gas बिलकुल यही crowd है, बस passengers molecules हैं और walls को जो shove वे देते हैं वही pressure है।

ideal gas point-like particles की एक crowd है जो कोई real volume नहीं घेरते, आपस में सिर्फ़ instantaneous collisions के दौरान force लगाते हैं, और बाकी समय straight lines में उड़ते हैं। कुछ भी उन्हें चिपकाता नहीं, इसलिए ideal gas में कोई potential energy of interaction होती ही नहीं।
यह रहा mental model: perfectly smooth marbles से भरा एक hall जो कभी attract नहीं करते और कभी deform नहीं होते। वे बस टकराते हैं और walls से elastically bounce करते हैं।

assumptions को नाम देना ज़रूरी है, क्योंकि हर आगे का result इन्हीं पर टिका है। molecules point masses हैं जिनका अपना volume container के मुक़ाबले negligible है। collisions के अलावा कोई intermolecular forces नहीं। और सारे collisions perfectly elastic हैं, तो कोई kinetic energy कभी lost नहीं होती।

कुछ और। collisions के बीच molecules straight lines में freely चलते हैं, actually colliding में negligible समय लगाते हैं; gas एक pure substance है जिसके molecules identical हैं; और gravity को ignore किया जाता है, तो density पूरे में uniform है। इनमें से कोई एक हटाइए और आप वापस real gas पर आ जाते हैं।

इस पूरे picture का payoff एक clean statement है: चूँकि कोई interaction energy नहीं है, ideal gas की सारी internal energy उसके molecules की motion की kinetic energy है। यही एक fact अगले दो subtopics को चलाता है।

board_events.text: Fails near condensation, at very high P (finite volume), at very low T (attractions win).
Hydrogen and helium stay near-ideal; water vapour and carbon dioxide deviate.
A fixed gas has just three state numbers: pressure, volume, absolute temperature.
The gas laws are bookkeeping for P, V, T; PV = nRT holds them all at once.

segments.text: <curious>So when does a real gas actually behave like this ideal?</curious> The answer is a regime: when its molecules are far apart and moving fast, that is, at low pressure and high temperature.

At low pressure the molecules are so spread out that the time they spend near each other, where attractions would matter, is negligible. At high temperature their kinetic energy so overwhelms any pull that the stickiness simply does not register.

The two panels say it at a glance. On the left, far apart and fast, the gas is ideal. On the right, squeezed and chilled, the molecules crowd together, attractions bite, and the gas eventually condenses.

So the idealisation fails in three places: near condensation, at very high pressure where the molecules' own volume stops being negligible, and at very low temperature where attractive forces take over. An ideal gas, note, can never condense at all.

Real examples make it concrete. Hydrogen and helium, small and weakly interacting, stay nearly ideal over a wide range. Water vapour near one hundred degrees Celsius, or carbon dioxide near room temperature, deviate noticeably.
One intuition to lock in: for a fixed amount of gas, only three numbers describe its state, the pressure, the volume, and the absolute temperature. Change any one and at least one other must respond.
The gas laws are just the bookkeeping rules for that trade-off when you hold one variable fixed. And the master equation, pressure times volume equals n R T, contains every one of them at once.
तो एक real gas असल में इस ideal जैसा कब behave करता है? जवाब एक regime है: जब उसके molecules दूर-दूर और तेज़ move कर रहे हों, यानी low pressure और high temperature पर।

low pressure पर molecules इतने फैले होते हैं कि एक-दूसरे के पास बिताया समय, जहाँ attractions matter करतीं, negligible है। high temperature पर उनकी kinetic energy किसी भी pull पर इतनी हावी होती है कि stickiness register ही नहीं होती।
दो panels एक नज़र में कह देते हैं। बाईं तरफ़, far apart and fast, gas ideal है। दाईं तरफ़, squeezed और chilled, molecules crowd करते हैं, attractions bite करती हैं, और gas आख़िर condense हो जाता है।

तो idealisation तीन जगह fail होती है: condensation के पास, बहुत high pressure पर जहाँ molecules का अपना volume negligible नहीं रहता, और बहुत low temperature पर जहाँ attractive forces हावी हो जाती हैं। ध्यान दीजिए, ideal gas कभी condense हो ही नहीं सकता।

real examples इसे concrete बनाते हैं। hydrogen और helium, छोटे और weakly interacting, एक wide range में लगभग ideal रहते हैं। water vapour करीब one hundred degrees Celsius पर, या carbon dioxide room temperature के पास, noticeably deviate करते हैं।

एक intuition पक्की कर लीजिए: एक fixed amount gas के लिए सिर्फ़ तीन numbers उसकी state बताते हैं, pressure, volume, और absolute temperature। किसी एक को बदलिए तो कम से कम एक और को respond करना ही पड़ता है।
gas laws बस उस trade-off के bookkeeping rules हैं जब आप एक variable fixed रखते हैं। और master equation, pressure into volume बराबर n R T, इन सबको एक साथ अपने अंदर रखता है।

board_events.text: Avogadro fixes the constant as nR, universal across gases.
R is universal: PV/nT approaches 8.314 J/mol/K for every gas as P approaches zero.

segments.text: <curious>The master equation is not handed down</curious>, we stitch it from the one-variable-fixed laws, changing the state in two stages so only one law acts at a time.
Here is the plan. We go from state one to state two through an intermediate state that shares the final pressure but keeps the initial temperature. Boyle rules the first leg, Charles the second.
Take a fixed mass of gas going from P one, V one, T one to the final P two, V two, T two. The intermediate sits at P two and V prime, still at temperature T one.
First leg, temperature fixed, so Boyle applies: P one V one equals P two V prime, which gives V prime as P one V one over P two.
Second leg, pressure now fixed at P two, so Charles applies: V prime over T one equals V two over T two, giving V prime as V two T one over T two.
Both legs gave an expression for V prime. Set them equal, cancel, and out drops the combined gas law: P V over T is the same before and after.
One step remains. Avogadro says volume grows with the number of moles, so the constant P V over T must scale with the amount of gas. Write it as n R, the same for every gas.
And there it is: P V over T equals n R, so pressure times volume equals n R T. Every one of the four laws is now a special case of this one relation.

R is called universal for a reason: measure P V over n T for any gas and let the pressure fall toward zero, and the answer approaches the same eight point three one four, be it hydrogen, oxygen, or argon.
master equation आसमान से नहीं आती, इसे one-variable-fixed laws से stitch किया जाता है, state को दो stages में बदलकर ताकि हर बार सिर्फ़ एक law act करे।
यह रहा plan। हम state one से state two तक एक intermediate state के ज़रिए जाते हैं जो final pressure share करता है पर initial temperature रखता है। पहले leg पर Boyle, दूसरे पर Charles।
एक fixed mass gas लीजिए जो P one, V one, T one से final P two, V two, T two की ओर जा रहा है। intermediate P two और V prime पर है, अब भी temperature T one पर।
पहला leg, temperature fixed, तो Boyle लागू होता है: P one V one बराबर P two V prime, जिससे V prime बनता है P one V one over P two।
दूसरा leg, pressure अब P two पर fixed, तो Charles लागू होता है: V prime over T one बराबर V two over T two, जिससे V prime बनता है V two T one over T two।
दोनों legs ने V prime के लिए expression दिया। इन्हें बराबर रखिए, cancel कीजिए, और combined gas law निकल आता है: P V over T पहले और बाद में एक जैसा है।
एक step बाक़ी है। Avogadro कहता है volume moles की संख्या के साथ बढ़ता है, तो constant P V over T को gas की मात्रा के साथ scale करना होगा। इसे n R लिखिए, हर gas के लिए एक ही।
और यह रहा: P V over T बराबर n R, तो pressure into volume बराबर n R T। चारों laws अब इसी एक relation के special cases हैं।
R को universal यूँ ही नहीं कहते: किसी भी gas के लिए P V over n T माप कर pressure को zero की ओर गिराइए, तो जवाब उसी eight point three one four के पास पहुँचता है, चाहे hydrogen हो, oxygen हो, या argon।

sections.title: The gas laws and the ideal gas equation

board_events.text: From four experimental laws to one master equation
R = 8.314 J/mol/K; kB = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K; NA = 6.022 x 10^23; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L.

segments.text: <curious>Let us gather the tools.</curious> Four experimental gas laws, each for a fixed mass of gas, and then the single master equation that contains them all.
Boyle's law, at constant temperature: pressure times volume is a constant, so P one V one equals P two V two.
Charles' law, at constant pressure: volume over temperature stays constant, so V one over T one equals V two over T two.
Gay-Lussac's pressure law, at constant volume: pressure over temperature is constant. And Avogadro's law: at fixed pressure and temperature, volume is proportional to the number of moles.

Stitch them together and P V over T is constant for a fixed mass, the combined law. Fix that constant as n R and you have the master relation: <excited>pressure times volume equals n R T.</excited> Recognise its equivalent forms instantly, in terms of mass over molar mass, in terms of molecule number and Boltzmann's constant, and the density form, pressure equals rho R T over M.

Two more, for mixtures and diffusion. Dalton's law: in a non-reacting mixture the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Graham's law: the rate of diffusion goes as one over the square root of the molar mass, so lighter gases diffuse faster.

Finally the constants to memorise. The universal gas constant R is eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin. Boltzmann's constant is R over Avogadro's number, one point three eight times ten to the minus twenty three joules per kelvin. And the molar volume at S T P, twenty two point four litres, works for every gas.
चलिए tools इकट्ठा करते हैं। चार experimental gas laws, हर एक fixed mass gas के लिए, और फिर वह single master equation जो इन सबको अपने अंदर रखती है।
Boyle law, constant temperature पर: pressure into volume एक constant है, तो P one V one बराबर P two V two।
Charles law, constant pressure पर: volume बटा temperature constant रहता है, तो V one over T one बराबर V two over T two।
Gay-Lussac का pressure law, constant volume पर: pressure बटा temperature constant है। और Avogadro law: fixed pressure और temperature पर, volume moles की संख्या के proportional है।

इन्हें जोड़िए तो fixed mass के लिए P V बटा T constant है, यह combined law है। उस constant को n R रखिए और आपके पास master relation है: pressure into volume बराबर n R T। इसके equivalent forms तुरंत पहचानिए, mass over molar mass में, molecule number और Boltzmann constant में, और density form, pressure बराबर rho R T over M।

mixtures और diffusion के लिए दो और। Dalton law: एक non-reacting mixture में total pressure partial pressures का sum है। Graham law: diffusion की rate one over square root of molar mass के जैसी है, तो हल्की gases तेज़ diffuse करती हैं।

आख़िर में constants जो याद करने हैं। universal gas constant R eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin है। Boltzmann constant R बटा Avogadro number है, one point three eight times ten to the minus twenty three joules per kelvin। और S T P पर molar volume, twenty two point four litres, हर gas के लिए काम करता है।

segments.text: A sealed cylinder holds two litres of an ideal gas at twenty seven degrees Celsius and one atmosphere. It is compressed to half a litre and simultaneously heated to one hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius. Find the new pressure.
The picture sets it up. Volume falls from two litres to half a litre, temperature rises, and both changes push the pressure upward.
Convert the temperatures to kelvin first. Twenty seven degrees becomes three hundred kelvin; one hundred twenty seven degrees becomes four hundred kelvin. Pressure starts at one atmosphere.
The amount of gas is fixed, so reach for the combined gas law, no need to compute moles at all. <whisper>For before-and-after problems, ratios beat plugging in n.</whisper>
Rearrange the combined law for the new pressure: P two equals P one times the volume ratio times the temperature ratio.
Substitute: one times four, from the volume shrinking fourfold, times four thirds from the temperature. That is about five point three atmospheres.

The new pressure is about five point three atmospheres. Notice we never converted litres to cubic metres, because volume units cancel inside a ratio. But the temperatures absolutely had to be in kelvin.

<curious>एक sealed cylinder</curious> में two litres ideal gas है twenty seven degrees Celsius और one atmosphere पर। इसे half a litre तक compress किया जाता है और साथ ही one hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius तक heat किया जाता है। नया pressure निकालिए।
picture इसे set कर देता है। volume two litres से half a litre तक गिरता है, temperature बढ़ता है, और दोनों बदलाव pressure को ऊपर धकेलते हैं।
पहले temperatures को kelvin में बदलिए। twenty seven degrees three hundred kelvin बनता है; one hundred twenty seven degrees four hundred kelvin। pressure one atmosphere से शुरू होता है।
gas की मात्रा fixed है, तो combined gas law उठाइए, moles निकालने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं। before-and-after problems के लिए ratios n plug करने से बेहतर हैं।
combined law को नए pressure के लिए rearrange कीजिए: P two बराबर P one into volume ratio into temperature ratio।
substitute कीजिए: one into four, volume के चौगुना घटने से, into four thirds temperature से। यह करीब five point three atmospheres है।

नया pressure करीब five point three atmospheres है। ध्यान दीजिए हमने litres को cubic metres में बदला ही नहीं, क्योंकि ratio के अंदर volume units cancel हो जाते हैं। पर temperatures को kelvin में होना ही था।

sections.title: Worked example: identify a gas from its density

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: density to molar mass
Speed method: at STP one mole occupies 22.4 L, so M = density x molar volume.
M = 28 g/mol: nitrogen (N2) or carbon monoxide (CO).
Trap: reading STP as 0 in M = rho R T / P gives M = 0. Never forget +273.
Pro-tip: at STP, shortcut through M = 22.4 x density and skip R, T, P entirely.

segments.text: <curious>At S T P a certain gas</curious> has a density of one point two five grams per litre. Identify its molar mass, and hence the likely gas.
Do not reach for the full formula. At S T P one mole of any ideal gas occupies twenty two point four litres, so the molar mass is simply the density times that molar volume.
So molar mass equals density times molar volume, one point two five grams per litre times twenty two point four litres per mole.
That multiplies out to twenty eight grams per mole.
A molar mass of twenty eight points to nitrogen or carbon monoxide, both of which weigh twenty eight grams per mole.

Here is the trap. The full formula, molar mass equals rho R T over P, tempts a full plug-in, and the killer mistake is reading S T P as zero degrees and forgetting the plus two hundred seventy three. That makes the temperature zero and the molar mass zero, an instant red flag.

So the pro-tip: <whisper>whenever you see S T P</whisper>, shortcut straight through molar mass equals twenty two point four times the density, and skip R, T and P altogether. It is faster and it cannot trip on the kelvin conversion.
S T P पर एक gas की density one point two five grams per litre है। इसकी molar mass पहचानिए, और उससे likely gas।
पूरी formula मत उठाइए। S T P पर किसी भी ideal gas का एक mole twenty two point four litres घेरता है, तो molar mass बस density into उस molar volume है।
तो molar mass बराबर density into molar volume, one point two five grams per litre into twenty two point four litres per mole।
यह गुणा करने पर twenty eight grams per mole निकलता है।
twenty eight की molar mass nitrogen या carbon monoxide की ओर इशारा करती है, दोनों का वज़न twenty eight grams per mole है।

यह रहा trap। पूरी formula, molar mass बराबर rho R T over P, full plug-in के लिए tempt करती है, और killer गलती है S T P को zero degrees पढ़ना और plus two hundred seventy three भूल जाना। इससे temperature zero और molar mass zero बन जाती है, तुरंत red flag।
तो pro-tip: जब भी S T P दिखे, सीधे molar mass बराबर twenty two point four into density से shortcut लीजिए, और R, T, P को पूरी तरह छोड़ दीजिए। यह तेज़ है और kelvin conversion पर trip नहीं कर सकता।

board_events.text: Dalton's law: each component acts as if the others were absent; partial pressures add.
Lesson: pressures add, masses do not; helium is lighter yet dominates by supplying the most moles.

segments.text: <curious>A rigid ten litre vessel</curious> holds four grams of oxygen and two grams of helium at three hundred kelvin. Find the total pressure on the walls, and the partial pressure of helium.
The key idea is in the picture: each gas independently fills the whole vessel, and their pressures simply add. Masses tell you nothing about pressure until you convert them to moles.
This is Dalton's law in action. In a non-reacting mixture, each component behaves as if the others were not there, so each contributes its own partial pressure and these add to the total.

So convert first. Four grams of oxygen over its molar mass thirty two is nought point one two five moles. Two grams of helium over four is nought point five moles. The total is nought point six two five moles.

Total pressure uses the total moles in the ideal gas equation, with the volume as ten to the minus two cubic metres. That gives about one point five six times ten to the five pascal, near one and a half atmospheres.

Helium's partial pressure is its mole fraction times the total. Its mole fraction is nought point five over nought point six two five, which is nought point eight. So its partial pressure is about one point two five times ten to the five pascal.

The lesson to carry away: each gas fills the whole vessel independently, and pressures add. But masses do not tell you pressure until they are turned into moles, and helium, though lighter, dominates the pressure because it supplies the most moles.
एक rigid ten litre vessel में four grams oxygen और two grams helium हैं three hundred kelvin पर। walls पर total pressure, और helium का partial pressure निकालिए।
key idea picture में है: हर gas independently पूरे vessel को भरती है, और उनके pressures बस जुड़ जाते हैं। masses आपको pressure के बारे में कुछ नहीं बताते जब तक आप उन्हें moles में न बदलें।
यह action में Dalton का law है। एक non-reacting mixture में, हर component ऐसे behave करता है जैसे बाकी हैं ही नहीं, तो हर एक अपना partial pressure देता है और ये जुड़कर total बनते हैं।

तो पहले convert कीजिए। four grams oxygen बटा उसकी molar mass thirty two, यह nought point one two five moles है। two grams helium बटा four, यह nought point five moles। total nought point six two five moles।

total pressure ideal gas equation में total moles इस्तेमाल करता है, volume ten to the minus two cubic metres के साथ। यह करीब one point five six times ten to the five pascal देता है, करीब डेढ़ atmosphere।

helium का partial pressure उसके mole fraction into total है। उसका mole fraction nought point five बटा nought point six two five, यानी nought point eight। तो उसका partial pressure करीब one point two five times ten to the five pascal।

साथ ले जाने वाला lesson: हर gas independently पूरे vessel को भरती है, और pressures जुड़ते हैं। पर masses आपको pressure नहीं बताते जब तक moles में न बदलें, और helium, हल्का होकर भी, pressure पर हावी है क्योंकि वह सबसे ज़्यादा moles देता है।

board_events.text: Master move: write total-moles conserved, initial equals final.

board_events.latex: n = \dfrac{P_0 V}{R T_0}+\dfrac{P_0 V}{R T_0}=\dfrac{2P_0 V}{R T_0}

board_events.text: Heating one half drives gas into the cooler bulb; write 'moles conserved' first and the algebra follows.

segments.text: <curious>Two identical bulbs</curious>, each of volume V, are joined by a thin tube and hold an ideal gas at a common pressure P nought and three hundred kelvin throughout. Now one bulb is warmed to four hundred kelvin while the other stays at three hundred. Find the new common pressure.

The whole problem turns on the picture. The bulbs stay connected, so the pressure equalises, but the total number of molecules never changes. Because the two bulbs are at different temperatures, they hold different numbers of moles at that common pressure.
So the master move is to write the conservation of total moles, once for the initial state and once for the final, and set them equal. Everything else is algebra.
Initially both bulbs are at temperature T nought, so the total moles are twice P nought V over R T nought.
Finally the common pressure is P, but one bulb is at T one and the other at T two, so the total moles are P V over R times the sum of one over T one and one over T two.
Conserve the moles, cancel V over R from both sides, and solve for P. It comes out as two P nought over T nought, times T one T two over the sum T one plus T two.
Put in three hundred, four hundred, and three hundred, and the answer is eight P nought over seven, about one point one four times the original pressure.

So heating one half drives gas into the cooler bulb, and the system settles at a higher common pressure. The whole problem is unlocked by the phrase total moles conserved; write that equation first and the algebra simply follows.

दो identical bulbs, हर एक volume V का, एक पतली tube से जुड़े हैं और एक ideal gas रखते हैं common pressure P nought और three hundred kelvin पर पूरे में। अब एक bulb को four hundred kelvin तक गरम किया जाता है जबकि दूसरा three hundred पर रहता है। नया common pressure निकालिए।

पूरा problem इस picture पर टिका है। bulbs जुड़े रहते हैं, तो pressure equalise हो जाता है, पर molecules की total संख्या कभी नहीं बदलती। चूँकि दोनों bulbs अलग temperatures पर हैं, वे उस common pressure पर अलग-अलग moles रखते हैं।
तो master move है total moles के conservation को लिखना, एक बार initial state के लिए और एक बार final के लिए, और उन्हें बराबर रखना। बाकी सब algebra है।
शुरू में दोनों bulbs temperature T nought पर हैं, तो total moles two into P nought V over R T nought हैं।
आख़िर में common pressure P है, पर एक bulb T one पर और दूसरा T two पर, तो total moles P V over R into one over T one plus one over T two हैं।
moles को conserve कीजिए, दोनों तरफ़ से V over R cancel कीजिए, और P के लिए solve कीजिए। यह निकलता है two P nought over T nought into T one T two over sum T one plus T two।
three hundred, four hundred, और three hundred रखिए, और जवाब eight P nought over seven है, original pressure का करीब one point one four गुना।

तो एक half को गरम करना gas को cooler bulb में धकेलता है, और system एक higher common pressure पर बैठ जाता है। पूरा problem total moles conserved इस phrase से खुल जाता है, वह equation पहले लिखिए और algebra अपने आप चल पड़ती है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: ideal gas and gas laws

board_events.text: The traps that cost the most marks here
The kelvin sin: the instant you see Celsius, add 273. P and V may be any consistent units; T must be absolute.
Mass is not moles: pressure, Dalton, and Avogadro all care about molecule count. Convert first.
Tag the constant variable: Charles (V/T) holds P fixed; the pressure law (P/T) holds V fixed.
Match R to units: 8.314 needs Pa and m^3; use 0.0821 L.atm/mol/K for litres and atmospheres.
Pro-tip: for fixed-mass before/after problems, never compute n; cancel constants in P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2.
Bridge: we asserted PV = nRT; the next subtopic derives it from molecules hitting the walls.

segments.text: <curious>This subtopic is a guaranteed scorer</curious>, so the traps are worth naming precisely. Five slips and one pro-tip.

First, the kelvin sin. Forgetting to convert Celsius to kelvin wrecks any gas-law calculation. Pressure and volume can stay in any consistent units inside a ratio, but temperature must be absolute. Build the reflex: the instant you see Celsius, add two hundred seventy three.

Second, mass is not moles. Pressure, Dalton's law, and Avogadro's law all care about the number of molecules, never the raw mass. Equal masses of two gases give different pressures, so always convert to moles first.

Third, do not mix up Charles' law and the pressure law. Charles, volume over temperature, holds at constant pressure; the pressure law, pressure over temperature, holds at constant volume. Tag the constant variable before you write anything down.

Fourth, do not treat units as optional in the master equation. If you use R as eight point three one four, pressure must be in pascal and volume in cubic metres. Prefer litres and atmospheres? Then switch R to zero point zero eight two one. Mismatching R with your units is a silent error.

And the pro-tip that saves the most time: for a fixed-mass before-and-after problem, never compute the number of moles. Just write P one V one over T one equals P two V two over T two and cancel whatever stays constant. It is faster and immune to unit slips, a genuine time-saver.

One thread to carry forward: so far we have simply asserted that a gas obeys pressure times volume equals n R T. The next subtopic finally asks why, deriving that very law from molecules bouncing off the walls.
यह subtopic एक guaranteed scorer है, तो traps को ठीक-ठीक नाम देना ज़रूरी है। पाँच slips और एक pro-tip।

पहला, kelvin sin। Celsius को kelvin में बदलना भूलना किसी भी gas-law calculation को बर्बाद कर देता है। pressure और volume ratio के अंदर किन्हीं consistent units में रह सकते हैं, पर temperature absolute होना चाहिए। reflex बनाइए, जैसे ही Celsius दिखे, two hundred seventy three जोड़िए।

दूसरा, mass moles नहीं है। pressure, Dalton law, और Avogadro law सब molecules की संख्या की परवाह करते हैं, कभी raw mass की नहीं। दो gases के equal masses अलग pressures देते हैं, तो हमेशा पहले moles में convert कीजिए।

तीसरा, Charles law और pressure law को मत मिलाइए। Charles, volume over temperature, constant pressure पर चलता है; pressure law, pressure over temperature, constant volume पर। कुछ लिखने से पहले constant variable को tag कीजिए।

चौथा, master equation में units को optional मत समझिए। अगर R eight point three one four इस्तेमाल करते हैं, तो pressure pascal में और volume cubic metres में होना चाहिए। litres और atmospheres पसंद हैं? तो R को zero point zero eight two one पर switch कीजिए। R को units के साथ mismatch करना एक silent error है।

और वह pro-tip जो सबसे ज़्यादा समय बचाती है: एक fixed-mass before-and-after problem के लिए, कभी moles मत निकालिए। बस P one V one over T one बराबर P two V two over T two लिखिए और जो भी constant रहे उसे cancel कीजिए। यह तेज़ है और unit slips से immune, एक असली time-saver।
एक thread आगे ले जाइए: अब तक हमने बस मान लिया कि gas pressure into volume बराबर n R T मानता है। अगला subtopic आख़िरकार पूछता है क्यों, इसी law को walls से टकराते molecules से derive करके।

board_events.text: Heat the gas: harder, more frequent hits, pressure rises. Halve the volume: twice as many hits, pressure doubles.
No collisions, no pressure. And pressure is a statistical average, meaningful only for enormous N.
Clausius, Maxwell, Boltzmann: from one set of postulates, the gas laws, specific heats, viscosity, and diffusion.

segments.text: <curious>In sub-topic one we asserted</curious> that a gas obeys pressure times volume equals n R T. Kinetic theory now answers the deeper question: why should pressure exist at all?

The triumph of the theory is that pressure, temperature, and the gas laws all fall out of Newton's laws applied to a crowd of bouncing molecules. It works because gas molecules are far apart: they fly freely and ignore one another, meeting only in brief collisions.

Picture a cricket ball machine firing balls at the back netting. One ball gives a tiny, jerky shove. But fire thousands per second from every angle and the net feels a steady, smooth, outward push, a pressure.

A gas does exactly this. Pressure is nothing more than the relentless drumbeat of molecules colliding with the container walls and rebounding. The wall does not feel individual hits; it feels the time-averaged force of an astronomical number of impacts.

This picture already answers exam questions. Heat the gas and the molecules move faster, hit harder and more often, so pressure rises. Squeeze it into half the volume and the same molecules strike the walls twice as often, so pressure doubles.
So keep the core statement: no collisions, no pressure. And pressure is a statistical average; it is only meaningful for an enormous number of molecules, never for a single one.

It took the nineteenth-century work of Clausius, Maxwell and Boltzmann to put this on a firm footing, and its reach is astonishing: from one set of assumptions it reproduces the gas laws, the specific heats, and links viscosity, conduction and diffusion back to molecular sizes.
sub-topic one में हमने मान लिया कि gas pressure into volume बराबर n R T मानता है। kinetic theory अब गहरा सवाल जवाब देती है: pressure existna ही क्यों चाहिए?

theory की जीत यह है कि pressure, temperature, और gas laws सब Newton के laws से निकलते हैं, जो एक bouncing molecules की crowd पर लगाए जाते हैं। यह इसलिए काम करता है क्योंकि gas molecules दूर-दूर होते हैं: वे freely उड़ते हैं और एक-दूसरे को ignore करते हैं, सिर्फ़ brief collisions में मिलते हैं।

एक cricket ball machine सोचिए जो back netting पर balls दागती है। एक ball एक tiny, jerky shove देती है। पर हज़ारों per second हर angle से दागिए और net को एक steady, smooth, outward push महसूस होता है, एक pressure।

gas बिलकुल यही करता है। pressure बस molecules की relentless drumbeat है जो container walls से टकराकर rebound करते हैं। wall individual hits महसूस नहीं करती; वह एक astronomical number of impacts की time-averaged force महसूस करती है।

यह picture पहले ही exam questions जवाब देता है। gas को heat कीजिए तो molecules तेज़ चलते हैं, harder और more often hit करते हैं, तो pressure बढ़ता है। इसे आधे volume में squeeze कीजिए और वही molecules walls पर दोगुनी बार strike करते हैं, तो pressure double हो जाता है।
तो core statement याद रखिए: no collisions, no pressure। और pressure एक statistical average है; यह सिर्फ़ molecules की भारी संख्या के लिए meaningful है, कभी किसी एक के लिए नहीं।

इसे firm footing पर रखने के लिए nineteenth-century के Clausius, Maxwell और Boltzmann का काम लगा, और इसकी reach हैरान करती है: <excited>एक ही set of assumptions से</excited> यह gas laws, specific heats reproduce करती है, और viscosity, conduction और diffusion को molecular sizes से जोड़ती है।

board_events.text: 4. All collisions perfectly elastic and instantaneous. 5. Motion is isotropic.
Elastic bounce, wall collisions as the only force, isotropy: each postulate carries a piece of the derivation.
Break one and the result fails: a charge adds a non-collisional force; a preferred wall kills isotropy; density brings back size and attraction.

segments.text: <curious>To turn this picture into equations</curious>, kinetic theory adopts a clean set of postulates, the rules of the idealised game. Every result that follows leans on them.

First, a gas is a very large number of identical molecules in constant, random motion in every direction. Second, a molecule's size is negligible compared with the spacing between molecules and with the container, so molecules are effectively point masses.

Third, molecules obey Newton's laws. Between collisions they travel in straight lines at constant velocity, exerting no force on one another, since there are no long-range intermolecular forces in the model.
Here they are together. Notice the random directions, the straight free flights, and the one molecule bouncing elastically off a wall.

Fourth, all collisions, molecule with molecule and molecule with wall, are perfectly elastic, conserving kinetic energy and momentum, and they are instantaneous. Fifth, the motion is isotropic: molecules are equally likely to move in any direction, so no direction is special.

See how much rides on these. The pressure derivation assumes elastic collisions so molecules rebound undiminished, wall collisions as the only force so gravity and attraction drop out, and isotropy so the mean square velocity is the same along every axis.

Break any one and the simple result fails. Put an electric field on charged molecules and a new non-collisional force appears; make one wall preferred and isotropy is lost; pack the gas densely and molecular size and attraction return. Kinetic theory is the physics of a dilute gas of neutral molecules.
इस picture को equations में बदलने के लिए kinetic theory postulates का एक clean set अपनाती है, idealised game के rules। हर आने वाला result इन्हीं पर टिका है।

पहला, gas identical molecules की बहुत बड़ी संख्या है जो हर दिशा में constant, random motion में हैं। दूसरा, एक molecule का size molecules के बीच spacing और container के मुक़ाबले negligible है, तो molecules effectively point masses हैं।

तीसरा, molecules Newton के laws मानते हैं। collisions के बीच वे constant velocity पर straight lines में चलते हैं, आपस में कोई force नहीं लगाते, क्योंकि model में कोई long-range intermolecular forces नहीं हैं।
यह रहे सब एक साथ। random directions, straight free flights, और एक molecule जो wall से elastically bounce कर रहा है, इन्हें notice कीजिए।

चौथा, सारे collisions, molecule से molecule और molecule से wall, perfectly elastic हैं, kinetic energy और momentum conserve करते हैं, और instantaneous हैं। पाँचवाँ, motion isotropic है: molecules किसी भी दिशा में move करने की equally likely हैं, तो कोई दिशा special नहीं।

देखिए इन पर कितना कुछ टिका है। pressure derivation मानता है elastic collisions ताकि molecules undiminished rebound करें, wall collisions ही एकमात्र force ताकि gravity और attraction हट जाएँ, और isotropy ताकि mean square velocity हर axis पर एक जैसी हो।

इनमें से कोई एक तोड़िए और simple result fail हो जाता है। charged molecules पर electric field लगाइए और एक नई non-collisional force आ जाती है; एक wall को preferred बनाइए और isotropy खो जाती है; gas को densely pack कीजिए और molecular size और attraction लौट आते हैं। <whisper>kinetic theory एक dilute gas of neutral molecules की physics है।</whisper>

segments.text: <curious>Now the derivation examiners love.</curious> From the postulates and Newton's laws, we show that pressure equals one third N over V times m times the mean square speed. Take N molecules of mass m in a cube of side l.
Focus on a single molecule with velocity components v x, v y, v z, and track its collisions with the shaded wall perpendicular to the x-axis, of area l squared.
The bounce is elastic, so the x-component reverses while v y and v z are untouched. The molecule's momentum changes by minus two m v x, so it delivers two m v x to the wall.
How often does it hit this wall? It must cross to the far wall and back, a round trip of two l at x-speed v x, so the time between two hits is two l over v x.
Force is momentum per unit time: two m v x every interval of two l over v x gives an average force of m v x squared over l from one molecule.
Sum over all N molecules. Each contributes its own m v x squared over l, so the total force is m over l times N times the mean square x-velocity.
Divide by the wall area l squared. The l cubed is just the volume, so pressure is m N over V times the mean square x-velocity.
Now invoke isotropy. Since no wall is special, each direction carries one third of the full speed squared. Substituting gives pressure equals one third rho v r m s squared.

Two things to notice. The box side l cancelled completely, so pressure depends only on number density, mass, and mean square speed, and holds for any container shape. The one third is the direct fingerprint of three-dimensional isotropy.

अब वह derivation जो examiners को पसंद है। postulates और Newton के laws से, हम दिखाते हैं कि pressure बराबर one third N over V into m into mean square speed। एक cube of side l में mass m के N molecules लीजिए।
एक single molecule पर focus कीजिए जिसके velocity components v x, v y, v z हैं, और x-axis के perpendicular shaded wall के साथ उसके collisions track कीजिए, area l squared का।
bounce elastic है, तो x-component उलट जाता है जबकि v y और v z अछूते रहते हैं। molecule का momentum minus two m v x बदलता है, तो यह wall को two m v x देता है।
यह wall को कितनी बार hit करता है? इसे दूर की wall तक जाकर वापस आना पड़ता है, two l का round trip x-speed v x पर, तो दो hits के बीच का time two l over v x है।
Force प्रति unit time momentum है: हर two l over v x interval में two m v x देने से एक molecule से m v x squared over l की average force मिलती है।
सारे N molecules पर sum कीजिए। हर एक अपना m v x squared over l देता है, तो total force m over l into N into mean square x-velocity है।
wall area l squared से divide कीजिए। l cubed बस volume है, तो pressure m N over V into mean square x-velocity है।
अब isotropy लगाइए। चूँकि कोई wall special नहीं, हर direction full speed squared का one third रखता है। substitute करने पर pressure बराबर one third rho v r m s squared।

दो बातें notice कीजिए। box side l पूरी तरह cancel हो गया, तो pressure सिर्फ़ number density, mass, और mean square speed पर depend करता है, और किसी भी container shape के लिए valid है। one third three-dimensional isotropy का सीधा fingerprint है।

sections.title: The kinetic equation and the pressure-energy bridge

board_events.text: The central results of this subtopic
Symbols: m is one molecule's mass (not the sample mass); n0 = N/V number density; vrms = root of the mean square speed; rho = Nm/V.
At fixed everything-else: P grows with N/V, with m, and with vrms squared, never with vrms itself.

segments.text: <curious>Let us gather the central results</curious> of this subtopic, the kinetic equation for pressure and the bridge from pressure to energy.
The kinetic equation for pressure: pressure equals one third times the number density times m times the mean square speed.
Two equivalent and very useful forms: pressure is one third rho v r m s squared, and pressure times volume is one third N m v r m s squared. Reach for the density form whenever density appears.
Mind the symbols. Here m is the mass of a single molecule, not the sample mass; N over V is the number density; v r m s is the root of the mean square speed; and rho is N m over V, the gas density.

Now the bridge. The total translational kinetic energy is N times one half m mean square speed. Rewriting the pressure relation to expose it gives pressure times volume equals two thirds of that energy.

So pressure is two thirds of the translational kinetic-energy density, and turned around, the total translational kinetic energy is three halves pressure times volume. This one line connects pressure to temperature in the next subtopic.

Finally the proportionalities to memorise, holding everything else fixed. Pressure grows with number density, with the molecular mass, and with the square of the r m s speed, never with the speed itself.
चलिए इस subtopic के central results इकट्ठा करते हैं, pressure के लिए kinetic equation और pressure से energy तक का bridge।
pressure के लिए kinetic equation: pressure बराबर one third into number density into m into mean square speed।
दो equivalent और बहुत useful forms: pressure one third rho v r m s squared है, और pressure into volume one third N m v r m s squared। density form वही है जो density दिखने पर उठाना चाहिए।
symbols का ध्यान रखिए। यहाँ m एक single molecule का mass है, sample mass नहीं; N over V number density है; v r m s mean square speed का root है; और rho, N m over V, gas की density है।
अब bridge। total translational kinetic energy N into one half m mean square speed है। pressure relation को उसे expose करने के लिए फिर से लिखने पर pressure into volume बराबर उस energy का two thirds।

तो pressure translational kinetic-energy density का two thirds है, और उल्टा करने पर, total translational kinetic energy three halves pressure into volume है। <whisper>यही एक line pressure को अगले subtopic में temperature से जोड़ती है।</whisper>
आख़िर में proportionalities जो याद करनी हैं, बाकी सब fixed रखते हुए। pressure number density के साथ बढ़ता है, molecular mass के साथ, और r m s speed के square के साथ, कभी speed के साथ नहीं।

sections.title: Worked example: rms speed from pressure and density

board_events.text: CBSE example: rms speed of oxygen
Reach for the density form: rho already bundles the molecular mass and number.
~480 m/s, comfortably faster than the speed of sound in air, as expected for molecular motion.
Takeaway: with P and rho given, vrms needs nothing else; the density form hides m and N inside rho.

segments.text: <curious>Oxygen gas is held</curious> at a pressure of one times ten to the five pascal with a density of one point three zero kilograms per cubic metre. Calculate the r m s speed of its molecules.
Reach straight for the density form of the kinetic equation. Because it already bundles the molecular mass and number into rho, we never need either separately.
Rearrange pressure equals one third rho v r m s squared for the speed: v r m s is the square root of three P over rho.
Substitute: three times one times ten to the five, over one point three zero, is about two point three one times ten to the five.
The square root is about four hundred eighty metres per second.
About four point eight times ten to the two metres per second, comfortably faster than the speed of sound in air, exactly what you expect for molecular motion.
The takeaway: when a problem hands you pressure and density, the r m s speed needs nothing else. The density form quietly hides the molecular mass and the molecule count inside rho.
oxygen gas one times ten to the five pascal pressure पर है density one point three zero kilograms per cubic metre के साथ। इसके molecules की r m s speed निकालिए।
सीधे kinetic equation का density form उठाइए। चूँकि यह molecular mass और number को पहले ही rho में bundle कर देता है, हमें दोनों अलग से कभी नहीं चाहिए।
pressure बराबर one third rho v r m s squared को speed के लिए rearrange कीजिए: v r m s three P over rho का square root है।
substitute कीजिए: three into one times ten to the five, बटा one point three zero, करीब two point three one times ten to the five है।
इसका square root करीब four hundred eighty metres per second है।
करीब four point eight times ten to the two metres per second, हवा में speed of sound से comfortably तेज़, ठीक वही जो molecular motion से expect करते हैं।
takeaway: जब problem pressure और density देता है, r m s speed को और कुछ नहीं चाहिए। density form molecular mass और molecule count को चुपचाप rho के अंदर छिपा देता है।

sections.title: Worked example: scaling the rms speed

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: triple the rms speed
At fixed density, pressure is proportional to the square of the rms speed.
Pressure becomes 9 times larger, not 3.
Trap: the careless answer '3 times' reads P as proportional to speed. Pressure follows v squared (from kinetic energy).
Rule: whenever a speed is scaled, square the factor before touching pressure or energy.

segments.text: <curious>A fixed quantity of gas</curious> is heated and stirred so that its r m s speed becomes three times its original value, while its density is kept unchanged. By what factor does the pressure change?
At fixed density, pressure is proportional to the square of the r m s speed. So the whole question is about what tripling the speed does to its square.
Write the ratio: the pressure ratio equals the square of the speed ratio.
Tripling the speed multiplies its square by three squared, which is nine.
So the pressure becomes nine times larger, not three.
Here is the trap. The careless answer is three times, reading pressure as proportional to the speed itself. But pressure follows the square of the speed, because it comes from kinetic energy.
So make it a rule: whenever a speed is scaled, square the factor before you touch pressure or energy. <whisper>That single reflex kills most of these traps.</whisper>
एक fixed quantity gas को heat और stir किया जाता है ताकि उसकी r m s speed original की three गुना हो जाए, जबकि density unchanged रखी जाती है। pressure किस factor से बदलता है?
fixed density पर, pressure r m s speed के square के proportional है। तो पूरा सवाल यह है कि speed को तिगुना करने से उसके square पर क्या होता है।
ratio लिखिए: pressure ratio speed ratio के square के बराबर है।
speed को तिगुना करने से उसका square three squared से multiply होता है, यानी nine।
तो pressure nine गुना बड़ा हो जाता है, three नहीं।
यह रहा trap। careless जवाब three times है, pressure को speed के proportional पढ़ना। पर pressure speed के square को follow करता है, क्योंकि यह kinetic energy से आता है।
तो इसे एक rule बना लीजिए: जब भी कोई speed scale हो, pressure या energy छूने से पहले factor को square कीजिए। यही एक reflex इनमें से ज़्यादातर traps खत्म कर देती है।

sections.title: Worked example: total kinetic energy from P and V

board_events.text: JEE Main example: energy without temperature
The pressure-energy relation: from PV = (2/3)E, the total KE is (3/2)PV.
Total ~450 J; per molecule ~1.1 x 10^-20 J. No temperature or molar mass needed.
The macroscopic pair (P, V) already encodes the total kinetic energy. That is the power of PV = (2/3)E.

segments.text: <curious>A rigid two litre vessel</curious> holds an ideal gas at a pressure of one point five times ten to the five pascal. Find the total translational kinetic energy of all its molecules. If it is monatomic with four times ten to the twenty two molecules, find the average kinetic energy per molecule.
The whole problem rides on the pressure-energy relation. From pressure times volume equals two thirds of the energy, the total kinetic energy is simply three halves pressure times volume.
So write the total energy as three halves pressure times volume.
Substitute: three halves times one point five times ten to the five times two times ten to the minus three cubic metres. That is three halves of three hundred, which is four hundred fifty joules.
Divide by the number of molecules, four times ten to the twenty two, and the average per molecule is about one point one times ten to the minus twenty joules.
Total translational kinetic energy four hundred fifty joules; average per molecule about one point one times ten to the minus twenty joules. Notice we never needed the temperature or the molar mass.
That is the power of pressure times volume equals two thirds energy: the macroscopic pair, pressure and volume, already encodes the total kinetic energy of the whole swarm.

एक rigid two litre vessel में ideal gas है one point five times ten to the five pascal pressure पर। इसके सारे molecules की total translational kinetic energy निकालिए। अगर यह monatomic है four times ten to the twenty two molecules के साथ, तो per molecule average kinetic energy निकालिए।
पूरा problem pressure-energy relation पर टिका है। pressure into volume बराबर energy का two thirds से, total kinetic energy बस three halves pressure into volume है।
तो total energy को three halves pressure into volume लिखिए।
substitute कीजिए: three halves into one point five times ten to the five into two times ten to the minus three cubic metres। यह three hundred का three halves है, यानी four hundred fifty joules।
molecules की संख्या, four times ten to the twenty two, से divide कीजिए और per molecule average करीब one point one times ten to the minus twenty joules है।

total translational kinetic energy four hundred fifty joules; per molecule average करीब one point one times ten to the minus twenty joules। ध्यान दीजिए हमें temperature या molar mass कभी नहीं चाहिए था।
यही pressure into volume बराबर two thirds energy की ताक़त है: macroscopic pair, pressure और volume, पूरे swarm की total kinetic energy को पहले ही encode कर देता है।

This IS the meaning of 1/3: energy shared over three directions, so each wall-pair gets a third. Strip isotropy, lose the factor.

segments.text: <curious>A thought experiment.</curious> Imagine a gas of N molecules confined to a cube but constrained so every molecule moves only along the x-axis, half in plus x and half in minus x, all at the same speed v. Find the pressure on the x-walls, on the side walls, and compare with a normal isotropic gas.
The picture frames it. On the left every molecule points along x, so only the x-walls get hit. On the right the isotropic gas spreads its motion over all three directions.
For part a, repeat the derivation but with no isotropy to invoke. The molecule's entire speed is in x, so the mean square x-velocity is the full v squared, not one third of it.
From the step just before the isotropy substitution, the x-wall pressure is N m over V times v squared.
For part b, no molecule has any y or z velocity, so no molecule ever strikes the side walls. Those walls feel zero pressure.
For part c, a real isotropic gas with the same numbers has one third N m over V v squared, so the directed gas pushes exactly three times as hard on the x-walls.

And this is the whole meaning of the one third. In a real gas each molecule's kinetic energy is shared equally among three directions, so any one pair of walls receives only a third of the if-everything-pointed-here pressure. Strip away isotropy and the factor simply disappears.
